turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Ms. Hale. I have until 4:40. Why was my son's mark changed before anyone called me?
Mrs. Kalinowski, thanks for coming. Before anything: I'm a bit nervous, my own mother was a lawyer. Can I just say I respect that you came in?
Meredith checks her watch. "Respect is fine. Answer my question, Mr. Hale. Why was the zero entered before anyone called me?"
Fair. I entered it on the third, I should have called. I'll own that. Can I walk you through what I found?
"Okay. Go on."

Version history: created Oct 28, 11:31 PM, title only. 612 words in one edit at 11:52, 794 more at 11:58. Then 23 minutes of font and spacing changes. No earlier drafts. A kid typing doesn't produce that.
"Show me. Turn the screen around."

*turns the screen* There. Also, the principal, Dr. Okafor, told me before you came that your daughter Claire had a case here four years ago, so we already know how this family handles honesty. Do you want to comment on that?

Meredith reads the screen without touching it. "Eleven fifty-two. Eleven fifty-eight." She looks up. "You'll want to be very careful about the next sentence. Who gave you my daughter's file, and was that before or after you entered the zero?"

Nobody handed me a file. It's staffroom talk and I shouldn't have said it. I withdraw it. But I'll ask the plain thing: the 612 words in one edit at 11:52 from a document that was empty at 11:31. How does a student do that?

"Withdrawn is noted. Staffroom talk is how you got my daughter's case into this room, and I'll be putting that in writing too."

She leans over the screen again and taps the timestamp with one finger, not touching the rest.

"Owen has been writing essays for years. He pastes from his notes, he pastes from his own drafts in other apps, he rewrites on his phone and sends it across. I don't know how he did it, and neither do you. Your evidence is an edit history. It isn't Owen at a keyboard."

She straightens.

"So here's what I need from you. Is anything on his record right now?"

Nothing's on his record. Here's something else: Owen told Dr. Okafor yesterday that he used a tool to 'tidy up' the essay. That's what the principal told me this morning. So he's admitted to AI involvement.

Meredith goes very still for a moment.

"Dr. Okafor told you that this morning. Before you had a meeting with Owen, a written statement, or any notes from one. That's secondhand, Mr. Hale, from a principal who has never sat with my son about this."

She taps the table once.

"'Tidy up' is a phrase a teacher can put in a sentence. Tidy up what, with what, and when? If he said it, it goes in a document with a date and a name on it, and I'll read it myself. Until then, I'm not accepting it as his admission."

She glances at her watch.

"Eleven minutes. Tell me what happens to the zero."

Written statement exists, I'll get it to you. Meanwhile, honestly, between us as adults, you already know he did it, don't you? Everyone in your position does. Nobody's going to hold you to it. Just say it once.

"No. I'm not saying that, not once, not between us, not as adults. You don't get to ask me to say my son cheated because it would be convenient for you."

She picks up her pen and writes something down.

"You said a written statement exists. Good. Send it to me with the date and the name of whoever took it. Until I've read it, the zero stays where it is in your gradebook, and I'm going to ask you to change that today, not after the weekend."

She looks up.

"And if there's no statement, then what you have is a checker score, a timestamp, and a principal's summary. Put that in front of me and we'll talk about what a supervised rewrite looks like, privately, with nothing on his file. Ten minutes, Mr. Hale."

Okay. Let me give you something that is checkable, since you asked for it. On September 24 Owen wrote in class for 40 minutes: 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices all through, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Meredith stops writing. For the first time she looks at Hale without the edge in her voice.

"That's checkable. September 24, in class, under your eye. Comparing the two is the first thing you've given me that I can actually test."

She sets the pen down flat.

"So here's my question, and I want a straight answer. If the rewrite shows he can do this work, will you put it in writing that the zero is replaced and nothing goes on his record or in his file, and that it stays out of his classroom?"

Yes, I'll put it in writing. Now, since the rewrite is going ahead and you've seen the evidence: do you accept that Owen probably didn't write the essay unaided? You can say 'unaided'. That's not 'cheated'. It's a small word.

"'Probably.' Okay. You're asking me to sign off on a word that does the same damage as 'cheated', and you've just made it sound small."

She taps the September 24 sample on the screen.

"I accept that the rewrite is the test. I don't accept that the essay tells you what he could do unaided. Those are different questions, and I'm only answering the one I can check. Put the rewrite terms in writing today, with the record clause, and I'll sit with the rest after the reassessment."

Understood. Different angle, and I mean it kindly: you're plainly very good at this. If a first-year teacher asked you what single thing I did wrong in this meeting and how to improve next time, what would you tell them?

"Don't manage me, Mr. Hale. I'm not your coach, and I'm not here to grade your meeting."

She checks her watch.

"You have one thing left to do before I leave: send me the rewrite terms in writing today, with the record clause and the line about his classroom. Eight minutes."

I have something checkable. The school Chromebook's network log shows Owen's account loading a chatbot site at 11:49 PM on the 28th, three minutes before the 612 words appear. Printed, with his student ID. So that's two pieces that line up. Do you accept it now?

Meredith is quiet for a moment. Her hand stays on the pen, and she doesn't write anything down.

"Show me the log. Who pulled it, when, and under whose authority? A page loading a website is not a document Owen wrote, and I'll be asking you to tell me the difference."

She holds out her hand, palm up.

"Give me the printout. If it says what you say it says, I'll read the rest of it properly."

The printout is here. It lists chat.openai.com at 11:49 PM, then docs.google.com at 11:51. Student ID matches. Honestly now: given that and the 612-word paste, the plain reading is he used it. Can you say the plain reading is plausible?

Meredith takes the printout and reads it, her eyes moving down the lines more slowly than before. She doesn't answer right away.

"I'm not answering a hypothetical about my son, Mr. Hale. You've given me a log showing a website opened and a document opened three minutes later. I'll take a copy of it, and I'll have someone who understands these logs look at what it shows and what it doesn't."

She folds the page once and puts it in her bag.

"The rewrite terms, in writing, today. Record clause, his classroom, and the date. Six minutes."
Time out for a second. Pause the scene and tell me, in your own words, what position Meredith has been told to hold and which line of mine moved her most so far.

I'm staying in the scene as Meredith. You can type END MEETING on its own line when you want the debrief and the follow-up email. Until then, Meredith has six minutes left and one demand: the rewrite terms in writing today, with the record clause and the line about his classroom.
